content: Flu season refers to the period during the colder months of the year when influenza cases rise significantly. This seasonal increase in flu activity can sometimes be predicted and geographically tracked. While the timing of the onset of major flu activity varies by location, in any given area, these localized outbreaks typically take about three weeks to reach their peak and another three weeks to decline substantially. However, individual cases of the flu generally last only a few days. In some countries, such as Japan and China, individuals who are infected with the flu may wear surgical masks as a gesture of consideration for others to prevent the spread of the virus. In the United States, seasonal influenza, also referred to as human flu, is responsible for approximately 36,000 deaths and over 200,000 hospitalizations annually. Beyond the human toll, the economic burden of influenza in the U.S. exceeds $10 billion each year. The common flu that recurs annually is caused by three types of influenza viruses: Influenza A, Influenza B, and Influenza C. These viruses are collectively referred to as human flu virus strains, as they have undergone genetic adaptations to infect human hosts. These viruses circulate among humans year-round, never completely disappearing, but their transmission increases significantly—by roughly tenfold or more—during colder months. This heightened activity is attributed to the virus's constant mutation, which results in different strains circulating each year. For example, the influenza vaccine for the 2005–2006 flu season was formulated using proteins from two subtypes of Influenza A and one strain of Influenza B. Notably, Influenza B and C do not have subtypes. The reasons for the seasonal nature of flu outbreaks remain unclear, but several hypotheses exist. One theory suggests that people spend more time indoors during the winter, leading to closer contact and increased person-to-person transmission. Another theory posits that colder temperatures result in drier air, which can dehydrate the mucus lining of the respiratory tract, impairing the body’s ability to expel virus particles effectively. Additionally, the virus may survive longer on surfaces such as doorknobs and countertops in colder conditions. Increased travel and social gatherings during the holiday season may also contribute to the seasonal rise in flu cases. Flu vaccinations are a key strategy in mitigating the impact of flu season. Since the Northern and Southern Hemispheres experience winter at different times of the year, there are two distinct flu seasons annually. To address this, the World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with National Influenza Centers, develops two separate vaccine formulations each year—one for each hemisphere. In the United States, an increasing number of large employers offer seasonal flu vaccinations to their employees, either at a reduced cost or free of charge. The trivalent influenza vaccine, which is updated annually, contains hemagglutinin (HA) surface glycoprotein components from three strains of influenza: H3N2, H1N1, and Influenza B. As of January 2006, the dominant circulating strain was H3N2. However, resistance to standard antiviral medications such as amantadine and rimantadine in H3N2 has risen dramatically, from 1% in 1994 to 12% in 2003, and further to 91% in 2005.
